extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, political economy, and social theory (general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted normative criteria and explanatory standards from Walter Bagehot's Physics and Politics about what early societies need to form, preserve, and progress as polities (origins of law, habit, leadership, unity, conflict, inheritance, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of law
rubrics_metrics.description: 'LAW--rigid, definite, concise law--is the primary want of early mankind; that which they need above anything else, that which is requisite before they can gain anything else.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot argues early humans first require fixed, definite law to provide order and anticipatory habits; without law other improvements cannot be reliably gained. Law creates steady expectations and is a prerequisite for civilisation rather than a later refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of government over quality in early times
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In early times the quantity of government is much more important than its quality. What you want is a comprehensive rule binding men together... What this rule is does not matter so much. A good rule is better than a bad one, but any rule is better than none.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For nascent societies securing any stable, comprehensive authority (making people act similarly and know what to expect) is more critical than whether the rule is well-designed; the immediate need is to create uniform behaviour and obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of Church and State (single government regulating all life)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To gain that obedience, the primary condition is the identity--not the union, but the sameness--of what we now call Church and State...king must be priest, and prophet king: the two must say the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot holds that early polities secure obedience by fusing spiritual and temporal authority so there is no divided message; differences between ecclesiastical and civil penalties must not be awakened. This unity produces the 'cake of custom' that hardens social habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impressive/ceremonial elements to secure obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The impressive elements of a polity are incomparably more important than its useful elements. How to get the obedience of men is the hard problem; what you do with that obedience is less critical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ceremony, visible authority, and ritualized forms (the 'impressive') create compliance; these may matter more than pragmatic usefulness in early societies because they establish and maintain the social mould and hereditary drill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary drill and habit formation (education into reflex acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted physiological account: repeated deliberate actions become 'organised into more or less unconscious, or reflex, operations'—the nervous system 'stores up' acquired actions so they are performed without volition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot (via Huxley) uses examples (soldier drill, reading aloud) to show education by repetition creates embodied habits that become transmissible social assets; institutionalised drill (custom, ritual, training) produces the stable dispositions necessary for civilisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of acquired faculties (inheritance of cultivated aptitudes)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a tendency...that the descendants of cultivated parents will have, by born nervous organisation, a greater aptitude for cultivation than the descendants of such as are not cultivated; and that this tendency augments...for many generations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing on Maudsley and contemporary thought, Bagehot treats the inheritance of acquired (or at least ancestrally stored) habits as a physical/social mechanism by which civilisation accumulates and advances across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conflict / natural selection in political development
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whatever may be said against the principle of 'natural selection' in other departments, there is no doubt of its predominance in early human history. The strongest killed out the weakest, as they could.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early polities and forms of government that conferred military or organisational advantage tended to survive; competition and conflict select for more effective social arrangements in the precarious pre-modern environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity/likeness as the basis of a nation
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A nation means a LIKE body of men, because of that likeness capable of acting together, and because of that likeness inclined to obey similar rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot emphasises cultural/social likeness (shared habits, customs, expectations) as the necessary condition for collective political action and obedience; nationhood depends on sufficient homogeneity enabling coordinated rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of oligarchy/elite as custodians of law and drill
rubrics_metrics.description: Early societies 'had then sole command over the primary social want. It alone knew the code of drill; it alone was obeyed; it alone could drill.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fixed law and drill are specialised knowledge, a close oligarchy or patriciate that preserves and applies that knowledge becomes essential to maintain the polity; elites transmit institutional memory and training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of free thought as a functional feature in early stages
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That this regime forbids free thought is not an evil; or rather, though an evil, it is the necessary basis for the greatest good; it is necessary for making the mould of civilisation, and hardening the soft fibre of early man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot provocatively argues that limiting intellectual freedom (uniform teaching, obedience) may be a pragmatic necessity in formative stages to enforce the habits and customs required for social stability and subsequent development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to create anticipatory habits and settled life (material and moral clock-work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive peoples 'neither knew nature, which is the clock-work of material civilisation, nor possessed a polity, which is a kind of clock-work to moral civilisation...the whole habit of steady but varied anticipation...must have been wholly foreign to theirs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civilisation depends on institutions (both material technologies like clocks and moral/political structures) that enable planning and predictable behaviour; creating these anticipatory frameworks is a central early task of polity-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress by increasing specialisation (development from general to special)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The development takes place in accordance with that law of increasing speciality and complexity of adaptation to external nature...that law, of progress from the general to the special in development which the appearance of nerve force amongst natural forces and the complexity of the nervous system of man both illustrate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bagehot frames civilisational progress as growing specialisation (skills, institutions, nervous organisation) that accumulates across generations—supporting arguments about transmitted aptitudes and differentiated social roles necessary for advanced polities.
